name: Commercial SAR/Optical ISR Constellation
representative_system: Composite: ICEYE SAR constellation + Maxar/Planet/BlackSky optical imagery

cost.display: ~$17M crowdfunded to buy Ukraine dedicated access to an ICEYE satellite; commercial tasking/subscription access runs separately (the US alone pays Maxar ~$300M/year for archive + tasking access)

key_facts.label: Coverage
key_facts.value: Global, on-demand tasking — not tied to airspace or front-line risk

key_facts.label: SAR advantage
key_facts.value: Radar imaging works through cloud cover and at night

key_facts.label: Access model
key_facts.value: Mostly commercial subscription/tasking, not a dedicated military constellation

short_role: Commercial imaging satellites — synthetic-aperture radar and optical — providing wide-area, all-weather intelligence without risking a crewed aircraft.
characteristics: SAR imaging (e.g. ICEYE) sees through cloud cover and at night, unlike optical-only imagery
No dedicated military constellation required — access is bought/subscribed from commercial operators
Feeds targeting, battle-damage assessment and the slower, multi-day pattern-of-life picture, not just single strikes
Access has proven politically contingent: a provider restricting access can degrade capability on short notice
employment_notes: The map's horizontal placement here is a convention, not a literal position — a satellite doesn't sit at a fixed distance from the front. It's placed in the strategic-rear band because that's the echelon it's tasked and analyzed from, not because of orbital geometry. In practice it feeds everything from single-strike targeting to the multi-day pattern-of-life picture that locates enemy positions.
contrast_vs_traditional: Wide-area, persistent overhead intelligence used to require a state actually operating a military reconnaissance satellite constellation — a capability only a handful of countries had. Access to commercial SAR and optical imagery has made a comparable capability available to a much smaller actor through subscription and crowdfunding rather than a national space program, while also making that access dependent on a commercial provider's business and political decisions in a way a sovereign satellite never would be.
